I think it’s not too crowded, I mean it’s a very open park, but it is a park – which has lots of vignettes and shade and things like that, and beautiful settings, beautiful scene of the river … of the city skyline. Plenty of restrooms [laughs], you know. And free water stations, free phone charging stations, in-and-out privileges, kids 10 and under free. I’ve taken some things from other events and some things we just decided to do on our own. I think our price point is very reasonable.

I think the volunteers and people in our city are generally very nice to people from out of town. … I like the fact that we card you and your wristband is your ID as well so you don’t have to deal with another line or getting a wristband if you want to drink. … And [Bunbury has] plenty of food options, great beer options.

What I think I learned [laughs], the hardest lesson I learned is – not that I hadn’t done events and I knew this was going to be hard – the execution of the event was flawless. We had a lot of people who thought we had been around a lot longer than our first year. But I really thought we’d have an easier time convincing people in year one to buy tickets. We did fine, we did fine – but we did not meet my expectation on ticket sales. It takes a while for people to really understand what an event is about and if they’re willing to risk spending that money [for] that experience. It took the first tens of thousands of people that came and shared things on their Facebook page and if they tweeted about it and [shared] pictures to get people talking about it and excited.

And you know, in that first year I’d run into even people that I knew and say, “Hey, I’m really excited about my new job!” And they’d say to me, “Well, what are you doing?”

“Like are you serious? You know me! I told you I’m starting a festival.”

Cincinnati Magazine Profile: Hip To Be S:
Cincinnati Magazine, March 2008. "Hip To Be Square" by Kathy Y. Wilson. A profile of Bill Donabedian as managing director of Fountain Square at 3CDC (Cincinnati Center City Development Corporation).

Bill was selected from a pool of 90 applicants to become the managing director of Fountain Square in Cincinnati. He was hired by Stephen Leeper, then president of 3CDC. Bill's job was to program the square — to make it Cincinnati's "living room" and bring it back to life after a $48 million renovation.

Bill described his management philosophy: "I don't wait for consensus. I would rather fail on my own accord, analyze the failure, understand it and then come back and try again. I would rather do that than to have a group of people deliberate over the decision for months because in that time you could have already tried the idea."

Bill programmed the square with a wide variety of events and activities. He started a broomball league, brought in ice skating, organized concerts, and created events that drew diverse crowds. He wanted Fountain Square to be a place where everyone felt welcome — from businesspeople to families to young professionals.

One notable incident was the "Poemgate" controversy involving poet Nikki Giovanni. Bill had booked Giovanni to read poetry at the square, but she used explicit language during her performance. The incident generated media attention and debate about programming choices for public spaces.

Another incident involved a UC vs. Ohio State game being shown on the video board. When asked to take it down by someone who felt it was inappropriate for the square, Bill refused, saying it was exactly the kind of thing that made the square a living room for the city.

Bill brought his event planning experience to the role, having previously co-founded the MidPoint Music Festival. His approach was to try things, learn from failures, and keep pushing forward. He wanted to make Fountain Square a destination, not just a pass-through space.

The article noted Bill's background: he grew up a military brat, attended McNicholas High School and Miami University, and got his MBA from Xavier. Before 3CDC, he worked in restaurants, at Ralph Lauren, Winston Financial, Active Inc., and Convergys. He co-founded MidPoint Music Festival with Sean Rhiney in 2001.
